title: Multistate Professional Responsibility Examination (MPRE)
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public MPRE subject-matter outline. Not a capture of past questions.

items.stem: A lawyer who is admitted to practice only in State A opens an office in State B and advises State B clients on State B law without seeking admission in State B. The lawyer has
options: acted properly, because federal law permits a lawyer admitted anywhere to practice in every state
engaged in the unauthorized practice of law, because a lawyer may not practice in a jurisdiction where the lawyer is not admitted absent a recognized exception
acted properly, because the lawyer charges no fee for the State B work
acted properly, because the clients and the matter are located in State B
items.explanation: Rule 5.5 bars a lawyer from practicing law in a jurisdiction where doing so violates the regulation of the legal profession there, so advising State B clients on State B law without admission is unauthorized practice.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A lawyer learns that another lawyer in the community forged a client's signature on a settlement agreement and then lied to the court about it. Under Rule 8.3, the lawyer
options: must inform the appropriate professional authority, because the conduct raises a substantial question as to the other lawyer's honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness as a lawyer
has no duty to act, because lawyers are not their colleagues' keepers
must report the conduct only if the affected client consents
must report the conduct only if the other lawyer has been convicted of a felony
items.explanation: Rule 8.3 requires a lawyer to report another lawyer's violation that raises a substantial question as to honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness, and forgery plus lying to a court plainly meets that test.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A lawyer wants to thank a nonlawyer marketing consultant who referred a personal-injury client by paying the consultant a percentage of the legal fee recovered in the case. The arrangement is
options: permissible if the client consents after full disclosure
permissible if the consultant is a full-time employee of the law firm
permissible if the percentage is reasonable in light of the work performed
prohibited, because a lawyer may not share legal fees with a nonlawyer as payment for a referral
items.explanation: Rule 5.4(a) forbids sharing legal fees with a nonlawyer, and the narrow exceptions do not include paying a percentage for a referral, so the arrangement is prohibited regardless of consent or reasonableness.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A lawyer wants to advertise that his firm wins 99 percent of its cases, a figure calculated by counting only the cases the firm won and ignoring the losses. The advertisement is
options: proper, because lawyer advertising is protected commercial speech
misleading and therefore prohibited, because it creates unjustified expectations about the results the lawyer can achieve
proper if the lawyer adds a disclaimer that every case is different
proper, because the lawyer did in fact win each of the counted cases
items.explanation: Rule 7.1 bars a false or misleading communication, and a statistic built by hiding the losses creates unjustified expectations, so the disclaimer does not cure the underlying misrepresentation.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A newly admitted associate accepts a complex tax-shelter matter without researching the area, telling the client that she will learn as she goes. The associate has
options: violated the duty of competence, which requires the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation
committed no violation, because a newly admitted lawyer is held to a lower standard of care
committed no violation, because the client knowingly hired an inexperienced lawyer
violated a duty only if the client suffered a measurable financial loss
items.explanation: Rule 1.1 requires competence regardless of experience, and taking a matter without the necessary research breaches that duty even before any harm materializes.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A lawyer has never provided free legal services to persons unable to pay. Which statement best describes the lawyer's obligation under Rule 6.1?
options: The lawyer is subject to discipline for failing to provide any pro bono services
The lawyer must provide at least fifty hours of pro bono service each year or be suspended
The lawyer must provide pro bono service only when a court appoints the lawyer to do so
The lawyer should aspire to provide pro bono service, but a lawyer is not subject to discipline for failing to meet that aspirational goal
items.explanation: Rule 6.1 states an aspirational goal rather than an enforceable minimum, so a lawyer who provides no pro bono service faces no discipline, though the rule urges service.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A lawyer negotiating the sale of his own car lies about the vehicle's accident history to the buyer, who is not a client. The lawyer has
options: committed no violation, because Rule 8.4 does not reach conduct outside the practice of law
committed no violation, because private business dealings are governed only by criminal law
committed misconduct, because Rule 8.4(c) prohibits a lawyer from engaging in dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation, even outside practice
committed misconduct only if the lie is later repeated in a legal proceeding
items.explanation: Rule 8.4(c) bans dishonest conduct whether or not it occurs in the practice of law, so a knowingly false statement in a private sale is misconduct by itself.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A lawyer admitted in State A and State B is suspended from practice in State A for mishandling client funds. State B authorities learn of the suspension. State B may
options: impose reciprocal discipline based on the State A sanction, even though the underlying conduct occurred in State A
not discipline the lawyer for conduct that occurred entirely in State A
act only after the lawyer applies for reinstatement in State A
discipline the lawyer only if the lawyer is also convicted of a crime
items.explanation: Rule 8.5 and the reciprocal-discipline doctrine let a state impose discipline based on a sanction imposed elsewhere, so State B may proceed even though the conduct occurred in State A.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A lawyer instructs a paralegal to meet with clients, evaluate their claims, and tell them what course of legal action to take. The lawyer has
options: acted properly, because a lawyer may delegate any task to a supervised nonlawyer
acted properly if the clients agree to speak with the paralegal
acted properly if the firm's malpractice insurer approves the practice
violated the rules, because a lawyer may not assist a nonlawyer in the unauthorized practice of law by allowing the paralegal to give legal advice
items.explanation: Rule 5.5 bars assisting a nonlawyer in the unauthorized practice of law, and having a paralegal give legal advice falls outside the tasks a nonlawyer may lawfully perform even under supervision.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: An applicant for admission to the bar leaves a past arrest off the bar application even though the application expressly asks about arrests. When the omission is discovered, the applicant may
options: not be denied admission, because conduct before admission is irrelevant to fitness
not be denied admission, because the charges were dropped
not be denied admission, because the arrest record was expunged
be denied admission for lack of candor, because a false statement on a bar application bears directly on fitness to practice law
items.explanation: Bar applicants owe a duty of candor, and omitting an arrest that the application asks about supports denial of admission because it reflects on present fitness to practice law.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A lawyer deposits a client's settlement funds into the lawyer's personal checking account and pays routine personal bills from that account while a fee dispute is pending. The lawyer has
options: acted properly, because the lawyer tracked the exact amount owed to the client
acted properly, because the client consented to the arrangement
commingled client funds in violation of the rules, which require that client funds be held in a separate trust account
acted properly, because the disputed amount was small relative to the lawyer's own funds
items.explanation: Rule 1.15 requires client funds to be held in a trust account; mixing them with personal money is commingling, and neither tracking nor consent cures the violation.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A solo practitioner is administratively suspended for failing to pay her annual bar dues but continues to accept new clients. The lawyer has
options: acted properly, because an administrative suspension is not a true suspension
engaged in the unauthorized practice of law, because a lawyer whose license is suspended for any reason may not continue to practice
acted properly, because the suspension lifts automatically once the dues are paid within thirty days
acted properly, because only a court may suspend a lawyer's license
items.explanation: A lawyer may not practice while suspended, and an administrative suspension is a suspension; continuing to take clients therefore constitutes the unauthorized practice of law.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: Two lawyers form a firm and wish to operate under the trade name Citywide Injury Attorneys rather than using their own surnames. Under the Rules, the firm
options: may use the trade name, because Rule 7.5 permits a lawyer to practice under a trade name that is not misleading
may not use a trade name under any circumstances
may use the trade name only if every lawyer in the firm is named in it
may use the trade name only with the permission of the state supreme court
items.explanation: Rule 7.5 permits trade names so long as they are not misleading, and nothing in the Rules forbids a firm from adopting a descriptive nonmisleading name.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A lawyer admitted only in State A agrees to represent a client in litigation pending in State B and seeks to appear in the State B court for that one case. The lawyer
options: may represent the client in State B if the lawyer is admitted pro hac vice or is otherwise authorized by the tribunal to appear
must be a permanent member of the State B bar to appear in any State B court
may appear automatically, because admission in one state permits practice in every state
may appear only if the client is a resident of State A
items.explanation: Rule 5.5 recognizes authorized temporary practice, including admission pro hac vice, so the out-of-state lawyer may appear when the tribunal grants permission.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: A lawyer serves part-time as a judge in a local court. May the lawyer represent clients in matters pending before that same court?
options: Yes, because the lawyer's judicial service is part-time only
Yes, because part-time judges may practice in any court, including their own
Yes, but only if the opposing party consents
No, because a part-time judge may not practice law before the court on which the judge serves
items.explanation: The roles of advocate and judge are incompatible, and the rules bar a part-time judge from practicing before the court on which the judge serves, regardless of consent.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Regulation of the Legal Profession

items.stem: In a civil case, the client directs the lawyer to accept a reasonable settlement offer, but the lawyer believes the case could yield a larger award at trial. The lawyer
options: may reject the offer, because litigation strategy is committed to the lawyer's professional judgment
may reject the offer, because the client's preference is only advisory
must abide by the client's decision to accept the settlement, because the decision whether to settle is for the client to make
may reject the offer until the client obtains a second legal opinion
items.explanation: Rule 1.2(a) reserves the decision whether to settle to the client, so the lawyer must follow the client's instruction even when the lawyer would prefer to litigate.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A client tells his lawyer that he intends to kill his former business partner next week. The lawyer
options: must keep the information confidential and may not warn anyone
may disclose the information to the extent necessary to prevent the reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm
must immediately notify the police and the intended victim
must withdraw from the representation and otherwise remain silent
items.explanation: Rule 1.6(b)(1) permits, but does not require, a lawyer to reveal information reasonably necessary to prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A client stops paying the lawyer's monthly bills, and the lawyer's withdrawal will not prejudice the client because a replacement lawyer can take over without harm. The lawyer
options: may withdraw only with leave of court in every case
may withdraw, because a client's failure to pay fees is a ground for withdrawal when it can be accomplished without material adverse effect on the client's interests
may not withdraw once representation has begun
may withdraw only if the client consents
items.explanation: Rule 1.16(b)(5) allows withdrawal when the client fails to meet an obligation to the lawyer and withdrawal causes no material adverse effect, so the lawyer may withdraw here.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A lawyer with a heavy caseload repeatedly misses filing deadlines in a client's case, causing the case to be dismissed. The lawyer has
options: violated the duty of diligence by failing to act with reasonable promptness and zeal in representing the client
committed no violation, because the heavy caseload is a sufficient excuse
committed no violation unless the client files a formal complaint
breached only an ethical aspiration, not an enforceable rule
items.explanation: Rule 1.3 requires reasonable diligence and promptness; a heavy caseload is no defense, so the missed deadlines breach a binding duty.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: Opposing counsel conveys a settlement offer to the lawyer, who does not tell the client because the lawyer thinks the offer is too low to merit a response. The lawyer has
options: violated the duty to communicate by failing to promptly inform the client of the offer
committed no violation, because the offer was too low to be worth the client's time
committed no violation, because settlement authority belongs to the lawyer
committed no violation, provided the lawyer discloses the offer before the case ends
items.explanation: Rule 1.4 requires a lawyer to promptly inform the client of significant developments, and a settlement offer is significant, so withholding it breaches the duty to communicate.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A lawyer agrees to represent a client in a contested divorce in exchange for a fee equal to thirty percent of any increase in the marital assets awarded to the client. The agreement is
options: permissible if the fee ultimately charged is reasonable
permissible if the client is informed of the arrangement in writing
permissible if the divorce is filed in federal court
prohibited, because the Rules forbid contingent fees in domestic relations matters
items.explanation: Rule 1.5(d)(1) prohibits contingent fees in domestic relations matters, so the agreement is forbidden even if the amount is reasonable and disclosed.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A former client refuses to pay the lawyer's bill, and the lawyer sues to collect the fee. In the collection suit, the lawyer
options: may never reveal confidential information, even to collect a fee
must obtain the former client's consent before filing suit
may reveal confidential information to the extent reasonably necessary to establish the claim for the fee
may reveal only the former client's name and address
items.explanation: Rule 1.6(b)(5) permits a lawyer to reveal information to the extent reasonably necessary to establish a claim for a fee, so the narrow disclosure is allowed.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A client pays a lawyer a $10,000 flat fee in advance for work not yet performed. The lawyer must
options: deposit the entire advance in the firm's operating account when received
deposit the unearned portion of the advance in a client trust account and withdraw it only as the work is earned
deposit the advance in a personal account, because the fee is earned on receipt
treat the advance as nonrefundable if the client signed a nonrefundable-fee clause
items.explanation: Rule 1.15 requires unearned fees to be held in trust and withdrawn only as earned, so the lawyer must keep the unearned portion in the client trust account.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: An elderly client with diminished mental capacity insists on giving her entire savings to a stranger who has been pressuring her. The lawyer should
options: immediately petition the court to appoint a guardian for the client
follow the client's instruction without question, because the client has the right to make poor decisions
withdraw from the representation and leave the client to her own devices
maintain, as far as possible, a normal client-lawyer relationship and may take reasonably necessary protective action because the client is at risk of substantial harm
items.explanation: Rule 1.14 directs the lawyer to preserve a normal relationship as far as possible while allowing protective action when the client is at risk, rather than ignoring or abandoning the client.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A lawyer proposes to lend a client $20,000 so the client can pay personal medical bills unrelated to the legal matter. The loan is
options: permissible if the client consents in writing after disclosure
permissible if the interest rate is reasonable
generally prohibited, because the Rules restrict a lawyer's financial assistance to a client to court costs and litigation expenses
permissible if the loan is documented by a promissory note
items.explanation: Rule 1.8(e) limits a lawyer's financial assistance to advancing court costs and litigation expenses, so a loan for personal bills is generally forbidden.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A lawyer who began representing a client last month now wishes to begin a consensual sexual relationship with that client. The lawyer
options: may begin the relationship if the client consents in writing
may not begin the relationship, because a lawyer may not have a sexual relationship with a current client unless the relationship predated the representation
may begin the relationship if it does not affect the quality of the representation
may begin the relationship, because it is a private personal matter
items.explanation: Rule 1.8(j) prohibits sexual relationships with current clients unless a consensual relationship existed before the representation, and it applies without regard to client consent.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A writer asks a lawyer to handle a lawsuit arising from a personal story, and the lawyer agrees to take the case in exchange for the movie rights to the story. The lawyer
options: may not acquire the media rights before the representation concludes, because Rule 1.8(d) prohibits that arrangement
may acquire the media rights if the writer consents in writing
may acquire the media rights if the price paid is reasonable
may acquire the media rights if a court approves the agreement
items.explanation: Rule 1.8(d) forbids a lawyer from acquiring media rights to a story about the representation before it concludes, regardless of consent, reasonableness, or court approval.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A lawyer holds funds in trust that both the client and a third person claim. The lawyer should
options: immediately pay the disputed funds to the client, who is the lawyer's client
immediately pay the disputed funds to the third person to avoid a dispute
keep the disputed funds separate until the dispute is resolved and may distribute the undisputed portions promptly
spend the disputed funds, because the client owns them
items.explanation: Rule 1.15(e) requires a lawyer to hold disputed funds separate until the dispute is resolved, while distributing the undisputed portions to those entitled to them.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A client asks the lawyer to design a set of transactions whose only purpose is to help the client evade federal income tax. The lawyer
options: may advise the client how to evade the tax, because the lawyer is not the client's keeper
may not counsel or assist the client in conduct the lawyer knows is criminal, including tax evasion
may assist if the client signs a written waiver of liability
may assist, because tax evasion is a civil rather than a criminal matter
items.explanation: Rule 1.2(d) forbids a lawyer from counseling or assisting a client in conduct the lawyer knows is criminal, and tax evasion is criminal regardless of any waiver.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A lawyer maintains a client trust account but keeps no ledger or individual records showing which funds belong to which client. The lawyer has
options: committed no violation, because the trust account is separate from the lawyer's personal funds
violated Rule 1.15 by failing to keep required records of client funds, even though no funds were commingled
violated the rule only if some of the client funds were lost
merely departed from a best practice that the rules do not require
items.explanation: Rule 1.15 requires a lawyer to keep complete records of client funds, so the absence of ledgers and individual records is itself a violation even without commingling.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - The Client-Lawyer Relationship

items.stem: A lawyer represents two clients who, after their interests become directly adverse in the same transaction, each want the same parcel of land. The lawyer
options: has a concurrent conflict of interest and may not continue representing both clients unless each gives informed consent and the lawyer reasonably believes the representation is not materially limited
may continue because both clients were informed of the joint representation at the outset
may continue because a lawyer is always permitted to represent multiple clients
may continue because the conflict is only a potential one
items.explanation: Rule 1.7 allows a concurrent conflict to be waived only with informed consent from each affected client and a reasonable belief that representation is not materially limited.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A lawyer who represented a corporation in negotiating a supply contract is now asked to represent a former employee suing that corporation over the same contract. The lawyer
options: may represent the employee, because the former client is a corporation rather than a natural person
may represent the employee, because the first matter has ended and the lawyer's knowledge is no longer confidential
may represent the employee if the corporation consents
may not represent the employee, because the new matter is substantially related to the former representation and materially adverse to the former client
items.explanation: Rule 1.9(b) bars representation materially adverse to a former client in a substantially related matter, and the same contract makes the two matters substantially related.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A lawyer personally is disqualified from a matter because of a former-client conflict. Another lawyer in the same firm has never worked on the matter. Under the general rule of imputation, the second lawyer
options: may take the matter, because conflicts are never imputed to other lawyers in a firm
may take the matter if the disqualified lawyer is only an associate
is also disqualified, because a conflict of one lawyer is generally imputed to the entire firm unless a recognized exception applies
may take the matter if the client consents, regardless of any other requirement
items.explanation: Rule 1.10(a) imputes one lawyer's disqualification to the whole firm, so the second lawyer is disqualified unless an exception permits otherwise.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A lawyer represents two co-defendants in a criminal case. One defendant decides to plead guilty and testify against the other. The lawyer
options: may continue representing both, because joint representation is always permitted in criminal cases
may continue if both clients consent after disclosure
must withdraw from representing both clients, because the divergent interests create a conflict that cannot reasonably be consented to
may continue and must keep each client's confidences from the other
items.explanation: When one client's cooperation is adverse to the other, the conflict cannot reasonably be consented to, so the lawyer must withdraw from both representations.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A person consults a lawyer about a business dispute but decides not to hire the lawyer and reveals damaging facts during the consultation. The lawyer then agrees to represent the other side in the same dispute. The lawyer
options: owes no duty to the person, because no attorney-client relationship was formed
may not represent the other side in the same or a substantially related matter, because the lawyer received disqualifying information from a prospective client
may represent the other side if the prospective client consents in writing
may represent the other side, because the consultation was free and brief
items.explanation: Rule 1.18 protects prospective clients, disqualifying a lawyer who received disqualifying information from later representing a materially adverse party in the same matter.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A client wants to buy a warehouse from a company in which the lawyer holds a substantial ownership interest. The lawyer
options: has a conflict between the lawyer's personal interests and the client's interests and may not proceed without informed consent and a reasonable belief that the representation is not materially limited
may proceed, because the lawyer disclosed the ownership interest
may proceed, because ordinary business dealings are not conflicts of interest
may proceed only if the lawyer charges no fee for the transaction
items.explanation: Rule 1.7(a)(2) treats a significant personal interest that risks materially limiting the representation as a conflict, requiring informed consent and a reasonable belief of competent representation.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: An insurer hires a lawyer to defend its insured. The insurer wants the case settled within policy limits, but the insured wants to go to trial to clear his name. The lawyer
options: must follow the insurer's instructions, because the insurer pays the legal fees
represents the insurer and must protect the insurer's financial interests
may let the insurer direct the defense without regard to the insured's wishes
represents the insured and, if the insurer's and insured's interests diverge, must protect the insured's interests and address the conflict
items.explanation: A defense lawyer hired by an insurer represents the insured, so when the insurer's interests diverge the lawyer must protect the insured and address the conflict rather than follow the payer.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A lawyer handling a client's trial is likely to be a necessary witness on a contested issue of fact. Under Rule 3.7, the lawyer
options: may both testify and act as trial advocate, because lawyers commonly testify
may act as both advocate and witness if the client consents
may act as both if the testimony favors the client
generally may not act as trial advocate, unless a recognized exception to Rule 3.7 applies
items.explanation: Rule 3.7 bars a lawyer from acting as advocate at a trial where the lawyer is likely to be a necessary witness, subject only to limited exceptions.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A lawyer served for months as the arbitrator in a commercial dispute. After the arbitration ends, a party asks the lawyer to represent it in later litigation over the same matter. The lawyer
options: may accept the representation, because the arbitration has concluded
may accept the representation if the arbitration outcome favored that party
may not represent anyone in connection with the matter in which the lawyer served as arbitrator, unless all parties to the proceeding give informed consent
may accept the representation, because arbitrators are not judges
items.explanation: Rule 1.12 extends the former-judge restriction to arbitrators and mediators, barring later representation in the same matter absent informed consent from all parties.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A client's wealthy parent offers to pay the lawyer's fees and asks the lawyer to send the parent regular progress reports containing confidential case information. The lawyer
options: may accept the payment and freely share confidential information with the parent
may not accept payment from a third party under any circumstances
may accept the payment if the client gives informed consent, the arrangement does not interfere with the lawyer's independence, and the client's information remains protected
may accept the payment if the parent signs a confidentiality agreement
items.explanation: Rule 1.8(f) permits third-party payment only with informed client consent, no interference with independence, and protection of client information, so the requested reports may not be shared.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A lawyer wants to buy an investment property owned by a current client. The transaction is
options: permissible if the purchase price is fair market value
permissible only if the terms are fair and fully disclosed in writing, the client is advised to seek independent counsel and gives informed consent, and the other requirements of Rule 1.8(a) are met
permissible if the client is an experienced real-estate investor
permissible, because a client may always consent to a conflict of interest
items.explanation: Rule 1.8(a) imposes specific conditions on business transactions with clients, including fair terms, written disclosure, advice to seek independent counsel, and informed consent.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A lawyer represents Company A in a contract dispute against Company B. Company B is also a current client of the same lawyer in an unrelated matter. The lawyer
options: may not represent Company A against Company B without the informed consent of both clients, because the representation is directly adverse to another current client
may represent Company A, because the two matters are unrelated
may represent Company A, because Company B is not a former client
may represent Company A if Company B does not object
items.explanation: Rule 1.7 forbids representation directly adverse to a current client unless both clients give informed consent, and the unrelatedness of the matters does not remove the conflict.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: After finishing a representation, a lawyer uses confidential information learned from the former client to benefit a new client and harm the former client. The lawyer
options: may use the information, because it has since become public
may use the information, because the former representation has ended
may use the information if the new client pays a higher fee
may not use the information to the former client's disadvantage, because Rule 1.9(c) prohibits it
items.explanation: Rule 1.9(c) forbids using a former client's confidential information to that client's disadvantage, and the end of the representation does not free the lawyer to disclose it.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A lawyer agrees to represent a client in a dispute while the lawyer owns a controlling interest in the opposing party. The lawyer
options: may proceed with the client's written consent
may not represent the client, because representing one side while controlling the opponent is a conflict that cannot reasonably be consented to
may proceed if the client is a sophisticated businessperson
may proceed, because ownership in another company is a private matter unrelated to ethics
items.explanation: A lawyer's control of the opposing party creates a conflict so severe that Rule 1.7(b) does not allow it, because no lawyer could reasonably believe the representation would be free of material limitation.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A lawyer who formerly worked for a government agency personally and substantially participated in an investigation of a company. The lawyer now works in private practice in the same matter. Under Rule 1.11, the lawyer
options: may not represent a private client in connection with that matter, unless the appropriate government agency gives informed consent
may represent the private client, because the lawyer no longer works for the government
may represent the private client, because government information is always public
may represent the private client if the client pays the usual hourly rate
items.explanation: Rule 1.11(a) bars a former government lawyer who participated personally and substantially in a matter from representing a private client in that matter without the agency's informed consent.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Conflicts of Interest

items.stem: A lawyer files a lawsuit that the lawyer knows has no basis in existing law and no arguable basis for extending or reversing the law. The lawyer has
options: acted properly, because a client may insist on filing any claim
acted properly, because every claim deserves its day in court
acted properly if the filing fee was paid
violated Rule 3.1, which prohibits a lawyer from bringing a proceeding without a basis in law and fact that is not frivolous
items.explanation: Rule 3.1 forbids asserting an action unless there is a basis in law and fact that is not frivolous, so a knowingly baseless suit is misconduct.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: A lawyer discovers that a client has testified falsely in a material matter and the lawyer knows the testimony was false. The lawyer must
options: keep the false testimony secret, because the duty of confidentiality forbids disclosure
do nothing, because the client stands to benefit from the testimony
take reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the tribunal if necessary, because Rule 3.3 requires candor toward the tribunal
immediately withdraw without telling the court anything
items.explanation: Rule 3.3 requires a lawyer who knows of false material evidence to take reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the tribunal if necessary, and confidentiality yields to that duty.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: A lawyer instructs a witness who has been properly served with a deposition subpoena not to appear for the deposition. The lawyer has
options: violated Rule 3.4 by unlawfully obstructing the opposing party's access to evidence
acted properly, because the lawyer may excuse a witness from attending
acted properly, because the deposition was unnecessary in the lawyer's view
acted properly if the client agrees to the instruction
items.explanation: Rule 3.4 prohibits unlawfully obstructing another party's access to evidence, and counseling a subpoenaed witness to skip a deposition does exactly that.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: On the eve of a criminal trial, the prosecutor holds a press conference and reveals the defendant's prior convictions to inflame the community. The prosecutor has
options: acted properly, because the convictions are a matter of public record
acted properly, because the press has a right to the information
acted properly, because no gag order was in place
violated Rule 3.6, because the statement has a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing an adjudicative proceeding
items.explanation: Rule 3.6 prohibits extrajudicial statements a lawyer knows or should know will have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing a proceeding, and inflaming the community meets that standard.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: A lawyer calls the opposing party directly to discuss settlement, knowing that the party is represented by counsel in the matter. The lawyer has
options: acted properly, because the opposing party is not the lawyer's client
acted properly, because the opposing lawyer was unavailable at the time
acted properly, because the communication was in writing
violated Rule 4.2, which prohibits communication about the matter with a person the lawyer knows is represented, absent consent or legal authorization
items.explanation: Rule 4.2 forbids a lawyer from communicating about the subject of the representation with a person the lawyer knows is represented, unless the other lawyer consents or the law permits it.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: While negotiating with an unrepresented opposing party, a lawyer explains the law and advises the party to accept the client's offer. The lawyer
options: may give the party accurate legal advice if the lawyer is careful
may give the advice if the party asks for it
must not state or imply that the lawyer is disinterested and must not give legal advice to the unrepresented party, whose interests may conflict with the client's
may give the advice if the party signs a written waiver
items.explanation: Rule 4.3 requires a lawyer dealing with an unrepresented person not to imply disinterest and not to give legal advice when the person's interests may conflict with the client's.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: During settlement negotiations, a lawyer knowingly makes a false statement of material fact to opposing counsel to gain an advantage. The lawyer has
options: acted properly, because negotiations are inherently adversarial
violated Rule 4.1, which prohibits knowingly making a false statement of material fact to a third person
acted properly if the client authorized the statement
acted properly if the false statement benefited the client
items.explanation: Rule 4.1 forbids a lawyer from knowingly making a false statement of material fact to a third person, and neither the adversarial setting nor client authorization excuses it.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: Responding to a proper document request, a lawyer fails to produce clearly responsive records that are in the client's possession. The lawyer has
options: violated Rule 3.4(d) by failing to make a reasonably diligent effort to comply with a proper discovery request
acted properly, because the records are unfavorable to the client
acted properly, because the lawyer may produce the records at trial instead
acted properly if the client asked the lawyer not to produce them
items.explanation: Rule 3.4(d) requires a lawyer to make a reasonably diligent effort to comply with a proper discovery request, and withholding responsive records breaches that duty regardless of the client's wishes.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: A lawyer represents a corporation. A mid-level employee asks the lawyer for personal advice about a claim the employee may have against the corporation. The lawyer
options: represents the corporation; when the employee's interests conflict with the corporation's, the lawyer must act in the corporation's best interest and may not give the employee personal legal advice
may represent the employee as well if the employee consents
represents the employee, because the employee asked the lawyer to give the advice
may represent the employee so long as the corporation pays the fees
items.explanation: Rule 1.13 makes the organization the client, so the lawyer must act in its interest and may not take on the employee as a separate client when their interests conflict.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: A lawyer mails a letter to the judge about a pending motion and does not send a copy to opposing counsel. The lawyer has
options: acted properly, because the lawyer also informed the client
acted properly, because the matter was urgent
acted properly, because opposing counsel would likely have agreed
violated Rule 3.5 by engaging in a prohibited ex parte communication with the judge about a pending matter
items.explanation: Rule 3.5 prohibits a lawyer from communicating ex parte with a judge about a pending matter when the law or a court order forbids it, so the letter breaches the rule.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: A lawyer learns before trial that a client intends to offer documentary evidence the lawyer knows is forged. The lawyer must
options: offer the evidence, because the client has the right to present a defense
offer the evidence and then expose the forgery in closing argument
refuse to offer the forged evidence and may seek to withdraw, because Rule 3.3 prohibits offering evidence the lawyer knows is false
destroy the forged document to prevent its use
items.explanation: Rule 3.3 bars a lawyer from offering evidence the lawyer knows is false, so the lawyer must refuse and may seek to withdraw rather than present it or destroy it.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: In closing argument, a lawyer refers to damaging facts that were never admitted into evidence, hoping to influence the jury. The lawyer has
options: acted properly, because the facts referred to are true
violated Rule 3.4(e) by alluding to matters the lawyer does not reasonably believe will be supported by admissible evidence
acted properly, because closing argument is not itself evidence
acted properly, because the judge did not interrupt the argument
items.explanation: Rule 3.4(e) forbids alluding to matters a lawyer does not reasonably believe will be supported by admissible evidence, and truth alone does not cure the improper argument.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: A lawyer knows that a document the client wants to submit to the court is false, but the client demands that it be offered. The lawyer
options: may offer the document, because the client has the right to submit whatever evidence the client chooses
may not offer evidence the lawyer knows is false, because Rule 3.3 prohibits knowingly making a false statement of fact to a tribunal
may offer the document if the client insists
may offer the document if the lawyer warns the court about it afterward
items.explanation: Rule 3.3 prohibits a lawyer from knowingly offering false evidence, and a client's demand does not override the duty of candor to the tribunal.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: A lawyer represents both the buyer and the seller in a real-estate transaction with both parties' informed consent. Before closing, the parties fall into a bitter dispute over the property. The lawyer
options: must withdraw from representing both parties, because continued joint representation would be materially limited by the conflict
may continue representing the buyer only
may continue representing whichever party pays the higher fee
must continue representing both parties until closing
items.explanation: When common representation of both sides breaks down, the lawyer must withdraw from both because the conflict will materially limit the representation and no longer can be consented to.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions

items.stem: A lawyer learns that a client is using the lawyer's negotiation statements to defraud a third party and that the lawyer's continued participation would assist the fraud. The lawyer
options: must not assist the client's fraud and, if necessary, must disclose material facts to the third person or withdraw from the representation
must keep the fraud confidential and continue negotiating on the client's behalf
must report the client to the police immediately
may continue, because a negotiation is not a statement of fact
items.explanation: Rule 4.1(b) bars a lawyer from failing to disclose a material fact when disclosure is necessary to avoid assisting a client's fraud, so the lawyer must disclose or withdraw.
items.reference: MPRE Subject Matter Outline - Litigation and Transactions
